summary: This Best Current Practice details the threats, attack consequences, security considerations, and best practices for browser-based applications that use OAuth 2.0.

eli5.summary: A guide to keeping your login keys safe when a website's code runs in your web browser.

subtitle: Which architecture to choose, and which tokens to trust the browser with, when a JavaScript app uses OAuth 2.0.

tldr.problem: Browser-based apps are public OAuth clients whose code can be hijacked by malicious JavaScript, such as through cross-site scripting. Once that happens, the attacker has the same privileges as the legitimate app.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes the attack scenarios and their consequences, then compares three architectures (a Backend for Frontend, a token-mediating backend, and a browser-only client) and the practices that are discouraged or deprecated. All of them use the Authorization Code grant with PKCE.
tldr.outcome: A BFF is strongly recommended for business, sensitive and personal-data applications. A browser-only OAuth client is not recommended for those, and the Implicit grant and Resource Owner Password Credentials grant MUST NOT be used.

today: RFC 10017 is a Best Current Practice published in August 2026 and has not been obsoleted or updated. It builds on the OAuth 2.0 security guidance in RFC 9700.

sections.title: Scope and History
sections.content:
This Best Current Practice describes architectural patterns for browser-based applications that act as OAuth 2.0 clients, and the security challenges they face. It focuses on JavaScript frontends, but the advice also applies to other code that runs in the browser, such as WebAssembly. Many recommendations derive from the OAuth 2.0 security BCP, RFC 9700, which this document expands and further restricts. Native apps are covered separately by RFC 8252.

Historically, the same-origin policy meant a browser app could not make the cross-origin POST needed by the Authorization Code grant, which motivated the Implicit grant from RFC 6749. That grant returns the access token in the URL fragment and has well-known weaknesses. With widespread CORS support, browser apps can now use the Authorization Code grant, and adding PKCE (RFC 7636) makes an intercepted authorization code useless to an attacker. The current best practice is therefore the Authorization Code grant with PKCE.

Applications with a frontend and API on a common domain may not need OAuth at all, and OpenID Connect-only setups are out of scope.
sections.eli5: Long ago, the safe way to get a key was awkward, so people used a shortcut that leaked keys. Now there is a better way that works fine in a browser.

sections.title: The Threat of Malicious JavaScript
sections.content:
Cross-site scripting or a compromised remote code file can let an attacker run code in the application's origin. That code has the same privileges as the legitimate application code. It can read origin-based storage such as localStorage and IndexedDB, send requests from the application's origin, and tamper with the app's own defenses. Prevention comes first: output encoding, limiting third-party scripts, Subresource Integrity, a nonce-based or hash-based Content Security Policy, and origin isolation. But no app is immune.

The RFC defines four attack scenarios:

  • Single-execution token theft: read the tokens once and send them away. Short lifetimes and refresh token rotation help.
  • Persistent token theft: keep stealing the latest tokens, for example on a 10-second interval. This defeats short lifetimes and rotation, since the app never uses an outdated refresh token and no reuse is detected.
  • Acquisition and extraction of new tokens: insert a hidden iframe, run a silent Authorization Code flow using the user's existing session, and read the code from the frame. DPoP does not stop this, because the attacker can use their own key pair.
  • Proxying requests via the user's browser: send requests from within the app, where the browser attaches cookies or tokens. This cannot be stopped by application-level measures.

The consequences are exploiting stolen refresh tokens (long-term impersonation), exploiting stolen access tokens (short-term impersonation), and client hijacking, which is less powerful because the attacker is limited by the client's policies, such as strict CORS.
sections.eli5: If a trickster gets into the clubhouse, they can do anything members can do, including ask the doorman for a brand new key. So the best plan is for the keys to never be in the clubhouse.

sections.title: Backend for Frontend (BFF)
sections.content:
In the BFF pattern, a server-side component of the frontend does all the OAuth work. It acts as a confidential OAuth client, keeps access and refresh tokens in a cookie-based session so the browser never sees them, and forwards every API request to the resource server with the right access token attached.

The flow: the app loads from a static host and asks the BFF whether a session exists. If not, the browser navigates to the BFF, which redirects to the authorization endpoint with PKCE. The BFF receives the authorization code, exchanges it with its client credentials, sets a session cookie, and sends the browser back to the app. Later API calls go to the BFF, which swaps the cookie for the access token.

Requirements include: the BFF MUST act as a confidential client and use the Authorization Code grant; cookies MUST have the Secure and HttpOnly flags, and SHOULD use SameSite=Strict, path /, no Domain attribute, and a __Host-Http- prefix; the BFF MUST implement CSRF defense (a custom request header with CORS is one option); and it MUST allowlist the destinations it proxies to so tokens cannot be leaked to arbitrary hosts.

Against malicious JavaScript, a BFF mitigates token theft and new-token acquisition. Only proxying requests (and so client hijacking) remains. The RFC says this architecture is strongly recommended for business applications, sensitive applications, and applications that handle personal data.
sections.eli5: A trusted receptionist holds your keys. When the browser needs something, it asks the receptionist, who uses the key for you and never hands it over.

sections.title: Token-Mediating Backend
sections.content:
A token-mediating backend also handles the OAuth flow as a confidential client and keeps the refresh token, but it hands the access token to the browser app, which then calls resource servers directly. It is lighter than a BFF because requests are not proxied.

Because the access token is exposed to the app, malicious code can steal it or ask the backend for the latest one. Refresh tokens are protected and new-token acquisition is blocked. The backend should be careful with cached tokens: if a cached access token has a superset of the scopes the frontend asked for, it SHOULD NOT return it, and SHOULD use the refresh token to request one with the smaller scope set instead.

Cookie and CSRF rules are the same as for a BFF, and sender-constrained tokens such as DPoP are hard to use here because responsibilities are split across two parties. The RFC strongly recommends evaluating a full BFF first.
sections.eli5: The receptionist hands you a day pass instead of doing everything for you. A trickster could take the day pass, but not the master key.

sections.title: Browser-Based OAuth Client
sections.content:
In the third pattern the browser app handles everything: it runs the Authorization Code flow with PKCE, posts the code to the token endpoint, stores the tokens, and calls resource servers directly. It is a public client with no credentials, so it is vulnerable to all four attack scenarios.

Key requirements:

  • Public browser clients MUST use PKCE, and authorization servers MUST support and enforce it for them.
  • Clients MUST register redirect URIs and use exact matches, and authorization servers MUST require an exact match.
  • Apps MUST prevent CSRF against the redirect URI, via PKCE, the state parameter, or the OpenID Connect nonce.
  • Authorization servers MUST NOT require client authentication using a shared secret, since a secret shipped to every user is not confidential.
  • Authorization servers and resource servers MUST send the CORS headers needed. Origins for postMessage MUST be verified.
  • For refresh tokens, servers MUST either rotate them on each use or use sender-constrained refresh tokens, MUST set a maximum lifetime or an inactivity expiry, and MUST NOT extend a rotated token's lifetime beyond the initial one. The RFC's example is a 10-minute access token with an 8-hour refresh token whose successors get shorter lifetimes (7 hours and 50 minutes next).

Defenses such as a Web Worker to hold the refresh token, or DPoP, help against token theft but not against the attacker running a new flow. The RFC says this architecture is not recommended for business applications, sensitive applications, and applications that handle personal data.
sections.eli5: The browser holds all the keys itself. That is simple, but if a trickster sneaks in, they can grab keys or ask for new ones.

sections.title: Discouraged and Deprecated Patterns
sections.content:
The RFC lists patterns that are no longer recommended.

  • Implicit grant: the token is returned in the URL fragment, where it can leak through redirect manipulation, browser history (which many browsers now sync across devices), injected scripts and third-party scripts. Authorization servers MUST NOT issue access tokens in the authorization response, and browser clients MUST NOT use the Implicit grant.
  • Resource Owner Password Credentials grant: MUST NOT be used. A redirect-based flow lets the server offer non-phishable authentication and single sign-on.
  • Service Worker handling the OAuth flow: tokens are isolated, but malicious code can unregister the Service Worker and then run its own flow in a new frame with no Service Worker attached. This pattern is not recommended.
  • Single-domain apps that use OAuth only as session management: often needlessly complex, though the RFC lists advantages of OAuth even there, such as future flexibility and centralized login.
sections.eli5: Some old shortcuts that people used to take are now known to be unsafe, so you should skip them.

sections.title: Token Storage in the Browser
sections.content:
Apps that hold tokens themselves must store them somewhere. The RFC compares the options, noting that none fully stops an attacker who runs a new authorization flow.

  • Cookies set from JavaScript: NOT RECOMMENDED, because the browser also sends them to the app's own server.
  • Service Worker or Web Worker: isolated from the app. A Service Worker MUST NOT keep tokens in persistent storage shared with the main window, such as IndexedDB. A common method keeps the refresh token in a Web Worker and hands only the access token to the app.
  • In memory: limits exposure to the current context, but closures can be undermined by prototype poisoning.
  • localStorage, sessionStorage, IndexedDB: reachable from any code in the origin. sessionStorage is tied to a tab, and IndexedDB is asynchronous.

Browser storage is not guaranteed to be encrypted at rest, so malware that reads a browser profile may find tokens.
sections.eli5: You can hide a key under the mat, in a pocket or in a locked box. Some hiding spots are harder to find, but a trickster inside the house can still search a lot of them.

sections.title: Further Security Guidance
sections.content:
Several practices apply to every architecture. Reduce token authority: short access token lifetimes, narrow scopes, and restricting a token to one resource using RFC 8707. Authorization servers SHOULD NOT put unused claims in ID Tokens.

Sender-constrained tokens, for example with DPoP (RFC 9449), make a token useless without a private key, ideally a non-exportable one from the Web Cryptography API. They help a token-mediating backend or a browser-only client but do not solve their basic limits, and the RFC notes non-exportable keys are not guaranteed to be protected on disk.

Clients that support multiple authorization servers should defend against mix-up attacks (see RFC 9700). Finally, deploy only one application per origin, so browser isolation and settings such as CORS and CSP are easier to apply. The RFC has no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: Give out small keys that expire fast and only open one door, and put your name on them so a stranger cannot use them.

items.title: Single-execution theft
items.text: Read the tokens once and send them to the attacker.

items.title: Persistent theft
items.text: Keep copying the latest tokens, defeating rotation.

items.title: New tokens
items.text: Run a silent flow in a hidden iframe to get independent tokens.

items.title: Request proxying
items.text: Send requests from inside the app; the browser attaches credentials.
